races.name: 10k
races.notes: A fitness check, not a peak. Start at 5:05 for the first 2 km, settle at 5:00, and if you still feel good at 7 km, push. Knee check: if it hurts during the warm-up or makes you change your stride, run it as an easy training run instead. The result sets the training paces for the Texel block.

races.name: Texel Trail
races.notes: Beach and dune trails: sand slows everyone down, so judge pace on the firm parts and run by effort in soft sand. Stretch goal, no stress: a strong finish beats a fast start. The volleyball match on Friday 5 Feb: play light, early to bed.

races.name: Beer Lovers Marathon
races.goal: Finish comfortably, together with the mates
races.notes: No time goal: run at easy-long-run effort and enjoy the tastings in moderation (water first!). Saturday at Nerdland: comfortable shoes, limit time on your feet, carb-rich dinner, early night.

races.name: Iron Viking
races.notes: A marathon with obstacles: expect 6-8 hours. Pace by effort, eat every 45 min, keep your grip fresh by not over-gripping on the run sections. Trail shoes with good drainage, gloves optional.

phases.name: 10k race week
phases.about: Training volume drops, one short session at race pace on Thursday keeps the legs sharp, and Saturday is a shake-out.

phases.name: Reset
phases.about: Easy running only. The 10k result is entered as new fitness and the Texel block is paced from it.

phases.name: Texel build
phases.focus: Long runs to 22 km, threshold, hills and dunes.
phases.about:
Twelve weeks that grow the long run from 12 to 22 km while adding one quality session a week.
Every fourth week is lighter so the body can absorb the work (and those weeks line up with your birthday and Christmas).
Strength twice a week from the start: Tuesday a circuit after the elliptical, Saturday after the easy run.
From January a fourth run comes in, because volleyball takes less of the week; strength moves to Tuesday (after the easy run) and Thursday (after the elliptical).
Specific work for Texel: dune long runs, hill repeats and race-pace blocks on sand.

phases.name: Texel taper
phases.about: Volume down by half, a little race pace on Wednesday, nothing on Thursday and Friday except the match.

phases.name: Marathon build
phases.focus: Long runs to 32 km, durability and fuelling.
phases.about:
After a recovery week, the long run grows from 16 to 32 km (peak on 19 April).
With no time goal, the quality work is about durability: tempo, hills and steady runs rather than marathon-pace sessions.
The wintersport week is a step-back week; Easter Monday hosts a big long run. Practise eating and drinking on every long run over 90 minutes.

phases.name: Marathon week
phases.focus: Rest, Nerdland, then 42 km with the mates.
phases.about: Short and easy. Saturday at the festival counts as rest day: sit when you can.

phases.name: Recovery & holiday
phases.about: Three weeks without structure: easy runs when you feel like it, hikes, swims. This is where a marathon is absorbed.

phases.name: Iron Viking build
phases.focus: Trail long runs to 33 km, strength, grip and obstacles.
phases.about:
Fifteen weeks to turn a marathon runner into an obstacle-course runner.
Long runs move to trails and grow to 33 km; Saturdays alternate trail runs with OCR circuits (run, burpees, hangs, carries).
The two weekly circuits (Tuesday and Thursday) keep the legs-and-pelvis work and add the grip and upper body that obstacles demand.
Every fourth week is lighter.

phases.name: Iron Viking week
phases.about: Easy running, no strength work after Tuesday.

easy.title: Easy {km} km
easy.why: Easy running builds the aerobic engine: more capillaries, more mitochondria, stronger tendons. Most of your running should feel this easy.

recovery.title: Recovery {km} km

strides.title: Easy {km} km + strides

long.title: Long run {km} km

long-trail.title: Long trail {km} km

long-finish.title: Long run {km} km, fast finish

progression.title: Progression {km} km
progression.why: A gentle first quality session: practises pace control and finishing strong without a hard interval session.

tempo.title: Tempo {reps} × {mins} min
tempo.why: Threshold running raises the pace you can hold for a long time without 'going into the red': the most useful engine work for 10 km up to the marathon.

intervals.title: Intervals {reps} × {dist}
intervals.why: Pushes your VO2max (the size of the engine). Hard but short; the jog recoveries matter as much as the reps.

hills.title: Hill repeats {reps} × {mins}
hills.why: Strength work disguised as running: builds power in calves, glutes and hips. Gold for dune trails and for Iron Viking.

fartlek.title: Fartlek {reps} × {mins}
fartlek.why: Playful speed. Lighter on the head than structured intervals, still gets the heart rate up.

steady.title: Steady {km} km
steady.why: Marathon-specific: teaches you to run efficiently at a steady effort for a long time.

race-pace.title: Race pace {reps} × {dist} km
race-pace.why: Locks the goal pace into your legs on the surface you'll race on.

sharpen.title: Sharpener {km} km
sharpen.why: Race week: keeps the legs sharp without tiring them.

shakeout.title: Shake-out {km} km
shakeout.why: Day-before routine: loosens the legs and calms the nerves.

trail.title: Trail {km} km
trail.why: Time on uneven ground: ankle strength, balance and confidence off-road.

ocr.title: OCR circuit {km} km
ocr.why: Iron Viking is a marathon with obstacles. Practise getting back into a running rhythm after strength efforts with tired arms.

strength.title: Strength {circuit}: {name}
strength.why: Stronger legs, hips and core make every stride cheaper and protect knees, shins and Achilles. The pelvis exercises teach your hips to keep the pelvis level and steer its rotation over the standing leg, which is where knee trouble often starts.

mobility.title: Mobility 15 min
mobility.why: Hips that rotate freely and ankles that bend let the pelvis and knees move the way they should when you run, so the lower back and knees don't have to make up for stiffness.

elliptical.title: Elliptical {mins} min

journal.title: The plan starts
journal.body:
Four races in eleven months: a 10k benchmark, Texel Trail (24 km), the Beer Lovers Marathon and Iron Viking (42 km with obstacles).

Starting point from the watch data: about two runs a week since late July, longest run 16.6 km, easy pace around 6:30-7:00/km.
The main point to work on: most runs were at heart-rate zone 3-4, which means "easy" days weren't easy.
The last two runs (21 and 25 October) were mostly in zone 2, which is exactly right. Keep doing that.

Fitness is estimated at VDOT 38 (predicts 52:15 for 10k). Sunday's 10k replaces that estimate and re-paces the Texel block.

journal.title: Knee niggle, almost gone
journal.body:
Some knee trouble in the week of 19 October; by today it is almost gone.
Today's easy run with strides became 30 min on the elliptical.

journal.title: Easier race week, and the elliptical joins the plan
journal.body:
This week is two easy runs (Thursday 5 km, Saturday shake-out) instead of a race-pace session, so the knee arrives at Sunday's 10k calm. If it hurts during the warm-up, run the 10k as an easy training run: no result is worth weeks off.

The elliptical and kettlebells at home are a real asset:
- Every easy and recovery run now shows an elliptical alternative (same heart-rate zone, about the same time). Use it whenever the knee or legs feel beaten up, or when the weather is grim.
- Long runs, quality sessions and the race-specific trail runs stay running: bones, tendons and feet only get race-ready from the impact of running, and Texel, the marathon and Iron Viking are all long days on your feet.
- The strength sessions are now a kettlebell circuit (goblet squats, swings, single-leg deadlifts, carries). Strong hips and thighs are the best protection for knees.
- Day after the 10k is an elliptical session instead of a recovery run.

journal.title: Thursday's easy run skipped
journal.body:
An extra hard volleyball training left the legs tired, so Thursday's easy 5 km didn't happen. In race week that's no problem, and don't make it up: fitness doesn't change in a few days, freshness does.

Saturday's shake-out matters a bit more now, because the last run was last Sunday. Run 4 km very easy and do the 3 strides to wake the legs up.
Tonight's match: play, but skip any extra jumping if you can, and get to bed early. If the knee felt the hard training, use the warm-up check on Sunday.

journal.title: Strength twice a week, pelvis control and Sunday mobility
journal.body:
From Tuesday 3 November: two 20-minute circuits a week, each straight after an easy run or the elliptical, plus 15 minutes of mobility on Sundays. The new Strength page has every exercise with how-to and why.

- When: in November and December on Tuesday (after 20-25 min on the elliptical) and Saturday (after the easy run). From January, Tuesday (after the easy run) and Thursday (after the elliptical). The Tuesday elliptical adds aerobic time without extra impact while the knee settles and volleyball is still weekly.
- What: legs, calves and core first, a little upper body. The circuits change with the season in four blocks: Foundation (now), Build (single-leg strength, first hops, sideways strength for Texel's sand), Marathon (endurance for calves and hips) and Iron Viking (grip, carries, crawls).
- Pelvis: every circuit has exercises that hold the pelvis level on one leg (hip hikes, single-leg bridges), steer its rotation over the standing leg (hip airplanes, single-leg deadlifts) and stop the trunk twisting along (Pallof press, dead bugs). Strong hips are also the best protection for the knee.
- Your own circuit is the starting point. Squats, push-ups, single-leg bridges, jumping jacks and kettlebell twists stay. Crunches became dead bugs, side crunches side planks, forward lunges reverse lunges, and two-legged ankle raises single-leg calf raises.
- Lighter weeks get 2 rounds instead of 3. Race weeks get a short, light circuit 4-5 days before the race, or none.
- Mobility: a 4-minute primer before every circuit and a 15-minute routine on Sundays for hips, ankles and upper back.

blocks.name: Foundation
blocks.focus: Learn the movements, pelvis control in every session.
blocks.about: Moderate weights, slow and controlled. Your own favourites stay in, the crunch-type exercises become running-specific core work, and every session has pelvis-control exercises. Single-leg work starts with support (a hand on the wall) and loses it as balance improves.

blocks.name: Build
blocks.focus: Heavier single-leg strength, first plyometrics, sideways strength for sand.
blocks.about: Four runs a week now, so the circuits get more specific: rear-foot-elevated split squats make the light bells feel heavy, swings add hip power, pogo hops start the spring work, and side lunges and Copenhagen planks prepare hips and groin for the dunes of Texel.

blocks.name: Marathon
blocks.focus: Keep the strength, build endurance in calves and hips for 42 km.
blocks.about: Long runs grow to 32 km, so the circuits don't try to add much strength: higher reps for calves and hips (they tire first late in a marathon), single-leg hops to keep the spring, carries for posture. In the peak and taper weeks rounds drop to keep the legs fresh.

blocks.name: Iron Viking
blocks.focus: Legs and core first; grip, pushing, pulling and crawling for the obstacles.
blocks.about: Iron Viking is a marathon with obstacles: walls, carries, crawls and hangs. The legs and pelvis work stays, and each circuit adds grip and upper-body work. If you can get to a pull-up bar (a playground works), finish with 3 dead hangs as long as you can hold them.

goblet-squat.name: Goblet squat
goblet-squat.how: Hold the bell by the horns at your chest, feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out. Sit down between your heels as deep as you can with a straight back, then stand up tall.
cues: Knees follow the toes, never inward
Whole foot stays on the floor
goblet-squat.why: Quads and glutes absorb the landing on every stride. Strong quads protect the knee and keep your stride from collapsing late in a long run.

reverse-lunge.name: Reverse lunge
reverse-lunge.how: Step one foot back and lower the back knee towards the floor, front shin about upright. Push through the front heel to come back. All reps on one leg, then switch.
cues: Front knee over the middle of the foot
Tall torso; a slight forward lean is fine
reverse-lunge.why: Running is a series of single-leg landings, so train one leg at a time. Stepping back is kinder on the knee than a forward lunge: there's no braking step.

split-squat.name: Rear-foot-elevated split squat
split-squat.how: Back foot laces-down on a couch or chair, front foot far enough forward that the shin stays fairly upright at the bottom. Bell at your chest. Lower straight down until the front thigh is about horizontal, drive back up.
cues: Most of the weight on the front leg
Pelvis level: the back hip doesn't drop or twist
Slow the first sessions; balance improves fast
split-squat.why: The strongest single-leg exercise you can do with light bells: with the back foot up, almost all the load is on one leg, so 9-11.5 kg becomes a real stimulus for quads and glutes.

step-up.name: Step-up with knee drive
step-up.kit: kettlebell, stairs or a sturdy box
step-up.how: Face a step about knee height (the second stair works). Put one foot up, push through that heel and stand tall, driving the other knee up to hip height. Lower slowly on the same leg. All reps one side, then switch.
cues: Push with the top leg; don't spring off the bottom foot
The knee-drive hip stays level or rises, never drops
step-up.why: The most running-like strength exercise: a single-leg push plus a knee drive, the same pattern as push-off and swing. Gold for dune climbs.

sl-rdl.name: Single-leg deadlift
sl-rdl.how: Stand on one leg, bell in the opposite hand. Hinge at the hip: chest forward and free leg back in one straight line, until you feel the back of the standing leg stretch. Squeeze the glute to stand up.
cues: Hips square to the floor: the free-leg hip must not open to the side
Soft knee on the standing leg
Fingertips on a wall if balance is the limit
sl-rdl.why: Hamstrings and glutes drive you forward. Keeping the pelvis square while the bell pulls on one side trains the anti-rotation your hips need at every landing.

kb-swing.name: Kettlebell swing
kb-swing.how: Feet a bit wider than hips, bell on the floor in front of you. Hike it back between your legs, then snap your hips forward so it floats to chest height. Let it fall back into the hinge and repeat. The arms are just ropes.
cues: A hip hinge, not a squat: shins stay fairly upright
Stand fully tall and squeeze the glutes at the top
Breathe out sharply at the top
kb-swing.why: Fast, powerful hip extension: the snap that drives you up a hill. Also builds the grip and back endurance Iron Viking needs.

sl-glute-bridge.name: Single-leg glute bridge
sl-glute-bridge.how: On your back, one foot flat close to your bottom, the other knee pulled to your chest. Drive through the heel to lift the hips until shoulder, hip and knee are in line; hold, lower slowly.
cues: Both hip bones at the same height: check with your hands
sl-glute-bridge.why: Glutes are the big propulsion muscles and they protect the knee. Holding the pelvis level on one leg is the hip's job at every footstrike.

sl-hip-thrust.name: Single-leg hip thrust
sl-hip-thrust.how: Upper back against the edge of the couch, one foot on the floor, the other knee pulled up. Lower your bottom towards the floor, then drive up through the heel until your hips are level with your knee.
cues: Full lockout with a glute squeeze at the top
sl-hip-thrust.why: A bigger range than the floor bridge, so the glute works harder through the hip angles used in running.

calf-raise.name: Single-leg calf raise
calf-raise.how: On one leg on the edge of a stair, heel hanging off, a hand on the wall for balance (bell in the other hand when the circuit says so). Rise as high as you can, then lower slowly until the heel is below the step.
cues: All the way up: the top is where calves are weakest
calf-raise.why: Your calves take six to eight times your body weight on every stride, more than any other running muscle. Strong calves and Achilles tendons are the best insurance against shin, calf and Achilles trouble, and give a springier push-off.

bent-knee-calf.name: Bent-knee calf raise
bent-knee-calf.how: Like the single-leg calf raise, but with the knee bent about 30 degrees and kept bent. Bell in the hand on the working side.
bent-knee-calf.why: With the knee bent, the soleus (the deep calf muscle) does the work. It's the hardest-working muscle in distance running and the one that tires in the last hour of a marathon.

lateral-lunge.name: Side lunge
lateral-lunge.how: From a wide stance, sit back and to one side, bending that knee while the other leg stays straight. Push back to the middle. Bell at your chest.
cues: Sit back into the hip, chest up
lateral-lunge.why: Sand, trails and obstacles throw you sideways. This trains the inner thigh and hip muscles that steady you on loose ground.

band-walk.name: Banded side walk
band-walk.how: Loop band just above the knees (around the feet is harder). Quarter squat, then step sideways keeping tension on the band, and back.
cues: Knees push out against the band
band-walk.why: Wakes up the glute medius, the muscle at the side of the hip that stops the pelvis dropping and the knee caving in when you land.

hip-airplane.name: Hip airplane
hip-airplane.how: Stand on one leg and hinge forward until torso and free leg are close to horizontal (hand on a wall or chair at first). Rotate your pelvis open: the free-leg hip turns up towards the ceiling. Then rotate it back down past level, towards the floor. Open and close is one rep.
cues: The rotation happens in the standing hip, not the back
Standing knee soft and pointing forward
hip-airplane.why: The pelvis-rotation exercise. At every step the pelvis turns over the standing leg, steered by the glutes and the deep hip rotators. Airplanes train that steering through the whole rotation, on one leg, under body weight: exactly where running needs control.

hip-hike.name: Hip hike
hip-hike.how: Stand side-on on the bottom stair on one leg, the other leg hanging free beside the step. Keeping both knees straight, let the free hip drop slowly below the step, then lift it back above level using the hip of the standing leg.
cues: Knees straight: the movement comes from the pelvis
No leaning sideways with the trunk
hip-hike.why: Trains the exact job of the glute medius at footstrike: catching the pelvis on the other side and lifting it level. Weakness here shows as a dropping hip, a caving knee and, often, knee or IT-band pain.

side-plank-lift.name: Side plank with leg lift
side-plank-lift.how: Side plank on your elbow, from the knees (easier) or feet. Straight line from head to knees or feet. Lift the top leg about 30 cm and lower it. Then the other side.
cues: Lift the leg slightly behind you, toes forward
side-plank-lift.why: The bottom side trains the side core that keeps you upright; the leg lift trains the top hip's glute medius. Together: a level pelvis when you land.

copenhagen.name: Copenhagen plank (short)
copenhagen.how: Side plank on your elbow with the top knee resting on the couch seat and the bottom leg free underneath. Lift your hips so your body is straight, and hold.
cues: Press the top knee down into the couch
Short holds at first: inner thighs get sore fast
copenhagen.why: Strong inner thighs pair with the outer hip to keep the pelvis level and stable, and lower the risk of groin trouble on uneven ground.

pallof-press.name: Pallof press
pallof-press.how: Anchor the band at chest height (closed door, stair railing, heavy table leg) and stand side-on to it, band in both hands at your chest. Press the hands straight out, hold 2 seconds while the band tries to twist you, bring them back. All reps one side, then turn around.
cues: Nothing rotates: hips and shoulders keep facing forward
Further from the anchor is harder
pallof-press.why: Anti-rotation: the core's main job in running is stopping the trunk from twisting along with arms and legs, so your energy goes forward instead of sideways.

band-chop.name: Half-kneeling band chop
band-chop.how: Anchor the band high. Kneel on the knee nearest the anchor, other foot forward. Pull the band diagonally from high beside you down across your body to the opposite hip, turning through the chest. Return slowly.
cues: The pelvis stays still; only the upper body turns
Squeeze the glute of the kneeling leg
band-chop.why: Running is shoulders turning against the hips. This trains that separation: the trunk rotates while the pelvis holds steady.

dead-bug.name: Dead bug
dead-bug.how: On your back, arms straight up, hips and knees bent 90 degrees. Press your lower back into the floor. Slowly lower the opposite arm and leg towards the floor as you breathe out, come back, switch.
cues: Lower back stays on the floor
Only go as low as you can without arching
dead-bug.why: The abs trained the way running uses them: keeping the pelvis still while arms and legs move in opposition. A steady pelvis means less arching of the lower back and a more efficient stride.

plank-taps.name: Plank shoulder taps
plank-taps.how: High plank on hands and toes, feet a bit wider than hips. Tap one hand to the opposite shoulder, put it back, switch.
plank-taps.why: Anti-rotation with alternating support, the same challenge as running's alternating legs, with some shoulder strength for free.

suitcase-carry.name: Suitcase carry
suitcase-carry.how: Hold the heavy bell in one hand by your side and walk tall: corridor, garden, or marching on the spot. Then the other hand.
cues: Don't lean towards or away from the bell
suitcase-carry.why: The side core and the hip on the free side keep you upright and the pelvis level, just like running tired. Builds grip for Iron Viking.

farmer-carry.name: Farmer carry
farmer-carry.how: A bell in each hand, walk tall for the time (or march on the spot).
cues: Tall posture, shoulders back and down
farmer-carry.why: Grip and posture under load: Iron Viking has carries, and grip goes before the legs on most obstacle courses.

kb-twist.name: Kettlebell ab twist
kb-twist.how: Sit with knees bent and heels on the floor, lean back a little with a straight back. Move the bell from one side of your hips to the other, touching the floor each side. One touch is one rep.
cues: Turn from the chest, not just the arms
kb-twist.why: Your favourite stays, slowed down: rotation strength for the trunk.

push-up.name: Push-up
push-up.how: Hands a little wider than the shoulders, body straight from head to heels. Lower your chest to a fist above the floor, push back up. Hands on the couch if form breaks down.
cues: One straight plank, no sagging hips
Elbows about 45 degrees from the body
push-up.why: Upper-body and core strength keep the arm swing relaxed and the posture tall late in a race, and push-ups are on every obstacle course.

kb-row.name: Kettlebell row
kb-row.how: One hand and knee on a chair or couch, back flat. Pull the bell from a hanging arm to your hip, elbow close to the body, lower slowly.
cues: Pull to the hip, not the chest
Squeeze the shoulder blade back at the top
kb-row.why: Upper back for posture and a strong arm swing, and pulling strength for Iron Viking's walls and ropes.

kb-press.name: Half-kneeling kettlebell press
kb-press.how: Kneel on one knee, bell in the hand on the kneeling side at your shoulder. Press it straight overhead, lower slowly.
cues: Squeeze the glute of the kneeling leg: no arching
Bicep ends next to the ear
kb-press.why: Shoulder strength with a core and hip challenge built in: the kneeling position stops you cheating with the lower back.

jumping-jacks.name: Jumping jacks
jumping-jacks.how: Jump the feet out and arms overhead, then back together. Light and quick on the balls of the feet.
cues: Stay on the balls of the feet
jumping-jacks.why: Easy elastic work that gets calves and Achilles used to bouncing. A first step towards pogo hops.

pogo-hops.name: Pogo hops
pogo-hops.how: Small, quick hops on the spot from the ankles, knees nearly straight, like skipping without a rope. As little ground contact as possible.
cues: Stop the set when contacts get slow or loud
pogo-hops.why: Plyometrics teach tendons to work like springs, which improves running economy: the same pace for less energy. Pogos are the gentlest way in.

sl-pogo.name: Single-leg pogo hops
sl-pogo.how: Pogo hops on one leg, a hand on the wall if needed.
cues: Pelvis level: the free hip doesn't drop
sl-pogo.why: All the spring on one leg, as in running, with pelvis control at the moment of landing.

bear-crawl.name: Bear crawl
bear-crawl.how: On hands and feet with the knees a hand's width above the floor. Crawl forward and back, opposite hand and foot moving together.
bear-crawl.why: A classic obstacle-race movement for core, shoulders and coordination. Iron Viking has several crawls.

burpee.name: Burpee
burpee.how: From standing, hands down, jump the feet back to a plank, chest to the floor, push up, jump the feet in and jump up.
cues: Step back instead of jumping if the knee complains
burpee.why: The obstacle-race penalty, and practice for getting up off the ground and running again.

leg-swings.name: Leg swings
leg-swings.how: Hold a wall. Swing one leg forward and back, then across the body and out to the side. Switch legs.
leg-swings.why: Loosens hip flexors, hamstrings and inner thighs in a running-like motion.

hip-cars.name: Hip circles (CARs)
hip-cars.how: On one leg, holding a wall. Lift the other knee in front, open it out to the side, take it behind you and down: the biggest slow circle the hip can draw while the pelvis and trunk stay still. Then the other direction.
cues: Pelvis still; only the thigh moves
hip-cars.why: Uses the hip's whole rotation range every session, so it's available when you run instead of being borrowed from the lower back or knee.

ninety-ninety.name: 90/90 hip switches
ninety-ninety.how: Sit with both knees bent 90 degrees, one leg in front of you, the other to the side. Keeping the feet on the floor, rotate both knees over to the other side. In the Sunday routine, also lean forward over the front shin.
cues: Sit tall; hands behind you if needed
ninety-ninety.why: Rotates each hip inward and outward: the range the pelvis needs to turn over the standing leg. Stiff hip rotation gets made up for by the lower back and knees.

worlds-greatest.name: World's greatest stretch
worlds-greatest.how: Big lunge step, both hands down inside the front foot. Drop the elbow towards the front ankle, then rotate that arm up towards the ceiling, eyes following the hand. Switch sides.
cues: Back knee off the floor (or down for easier)
worlds-greatest.why: Hip flexors, hamstrings, groin and upper back in one move.

hip-flexor-stretch.name: Half-kneeling hip flexor stretch
hip-flexor-stretch.how: Kneel on one knee on a cushion, other foot forward. Tuck your tailbone under and squeeze the glute of the kneeling leg until you feel a stretch at the front of that hip. Reach that arm up and slightly over.
cues: Tuck the pelvis before you lean forward
hip-flexor-stretch.why: Tight hip flexors tip the pelvis forward and shorten the stride. Tucking the pelvis puts the stretch where it should be.

open-book.name: Open book
open-book.how: Lie on your side, knees bent up to hip height, arms straight out in front. Open the top arm up and over to the other side, eyes following, knees together on the floor.
open-book.why: Upper-back rotation lets the shoulders counter-rotate freely, so the lower back and pelvis don't have to.

ankle-rocks.name: Knee-to-wall ankle rocks
ankle-rocks.how: Foot a hand's width from a wall. Drive the knee forward to touch the wall over the toes, heel down. Move the foot back when it's easy.
cues: Knee goes over the middle toes
ankle-rocks.why: Ankle range: a stiff ankle makes the knee and foot roll inward on landing.

calf-stretch.name: Calf stretch
calf-stretch.how: Hands on a wall, one leg back with the heel down. Straight knee first (upper calf), then bend the back knee a little (deep calf).
calf-stretch.why: Keeps both calf muscles supple after the strength and spring work.

figure-four.name: Figure-4 glute stretch
figure-four.how: On your back, ankle on the opposite knee, pull the bottom leg towards you.
cues: Push the crossed knee gently away
figure-four.why: Releases the deep hip rotators that steer the pelvis on every stride.

adductor-rockback.name: Adductor rock-back
adductor-rockback.how: On hands and knees, one leg straight out to the side, foot flat. Rock your hips back towards the heels and forward again.
cues: Rock as far as is comfortable
adductor-rockback.why: Inner-thigh mobility for side steps, sand and obstacles.

deep-squat-hold.name: Deep squat hold
deep-squat-hold.how: Hold a light bell at your chest as a counterweight and sit in your deepest squat, heels down. Gently push the knees out with your elbows.
cues: Heels down (a book under them is fine)
deep-squat-hold.why: Hips, ankles and back in a position everyday life rarely visits.
